requirements.heading: UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization
requirements.text: See [RFC5198] for a discussion of Unicode normalization; normalization form NFC [UNF] SHOULD be used.

requirements.heading: UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization
requirements.text: The NFKC normalization form [UNF] SHOULD NOT be used because it may lose information that is needed to correctly spell some names in some unusual circumstances.

requirements.heading: Use of 8-bit UTF-8 in Message-IDs
requirements.text: Implementers of Message-ID generation algorithms MAY prefer to restrain their output to ASCII since that has some advantages, such as when constructing "In-reply-to:" and "References:" header fields in mailing-list threads where some senders use internationalized addresses and others do not.

requirements.heading: Use of MIME Encoded-Words
requirements.text: Accordingly, encoded-words SHOULD NOT be used when generating header fields for messages employing this extension.

requirements.heading: Use of MIME Encoded-Words
requirements.text: Agents MAY, when incorporating material from another message, convert encoded-word use to direct use of UTF-8.

requirements.heading: Use of MIME Encoded-Words
requirements.text: Processors that elect to decode encoded-words MUST NOT generate syntactically invalid fields.

requirements.heading: The message/global Media Type
requirements.text: Internationalized messages in this format MUST only be transmitted as authorized by [RFC6531] or within a non-SMTP environment that supports these messages.

requirements.heading: The message/global Media Type
requirements.text: If an object of this type is sent to a 7-bit-only system, it MUST have an appropriate content-transfer-encoding applied.

requirements.heading: The message/global Media Type
requirements.text: An 8-bit or binary content-transfer- encoding SHOULD be used unless this media type is sent over a 7-bit-only transport.

requirements.heading: Security Considerations
requirements.text: As specified in [RFC5322], each line of characters MUST be no more than 998 octets, excluding the CRLF.
